subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

section_titles: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
periods.activity_title: Seeds, Sweets, and the Magic of Hidden Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Perform the hidden-seed magic trick with friends; write the number of hidden seeds in the table for six total-and-visible pairs.
Draw the number of dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 balushahi – 5 balushahi; complete the number sentences.
Card Game: shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; take turns opening one card; keep any three cards that form an addition or subtraction statement.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces Nani Maa's magic trick: show a fixed count of seeds, hide some under a handkerchief, reveal the rest, and ask children to work out the hidden amount. Children perform the trick in pairs with actual seeds or counters, filling in Let us Do, p.29 ("Perform the hidden-seed magic trick with friends; write the number of hidden seeds....") for all six pairs.

Shift to the balushahi context. Each child draws tens-frame dots for 7+5 and then for 7–5 on their slate or paper, following Let us Do, p.30 ("Draw the number of dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 balushahi – 5 balushahi...."). The teacher draws attention to the fact that the same two quantities appear in both sentences — addition and subtraction are two sides of one relationship.

The Card Game from Let us Play, p.31 ("Card Game: shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; take turns opening one card; keep any three cards....") runs in groups of three. Each trio shuffles a set of number cards, draws in turn, and keeps any three that form a valid addition or subtraction statement. The teacher circulates, listening for children who notice that the same three numbers can make more than one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often see subtraction as strictly 'taking away' and do not yet connect it to missing-addend thinking; the seed trick foregrounds this idea in a playful, concrete way. When children draw tens-frame dots for 7+5 and 7–5, press them to say aloud what stays the same across the two sentences. Watch for children in the card game who only look for addition — prompt them to turn any addition triple into a subtraction sentence.
materials: Four sets of number cards 1–10 per group

section_titles: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
periods.activity_title: From Tens Frames to the Bead String

tasks_in_class.description: Use the tens frame to solve: (a) 6+8 (b) 5+10 (c) 9–6 (d) 18–9.
Nandini and Chirag have 22 stamps; Nani Maa's brother gives 30 more — find the total using the ginladi.
A frog is at 7 and jumps 10 beads at a time — mark the beads it will land on and write the numbers.

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do, p.31 ("Use the tens frame to solve: (a) 6+8 (b) 5+10 (c) 9–6 (d) 18–9....") individually on their slates, drawing dots in the tens frame for each expression. A brief whole-class check surfaces any confusion between filling one frame and filling two.

The teacher introduces the ginladi (bead string) using a class bead string or a drawn number line on the board. Three characters from the stamp story each show a different jump strategy for adding; the teacher models all three. Children then solve Let us Do, p.32 ("Nandini and Chirag have 22 stamps; Nani Maa's brother gives 30 more — find the total using the ginladi....") on their own number lines, trying at least two strategies.

Children work on Let us Do Q2, p.34 ("A frog is at 7 and jumps 10 beads at a time — mark the beads it will land on and write the numbers...."), marking each landing bead and writing the sequence. Partners compare their lists and look for what changes and what stays the same with each jump of 10.

periods.teacher_notes: The tens-frame work on addition and subtraction within 20 underpins the ginladi work — both models show quantity as a structured set. Children who jump to adding in ones on the ginladi should be encouraged to try a jump-to-ten first, then count on, as the stamp characters demonstrate. A common slip is forgetting to count the starting position as zero rather than one — watch for this when children mark frog landings.
materials: Class bead string or rope with 100 beads, or a large drawn number line (0–100)
Tens-frame sheets or drawn tens frames

section_titles: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100

tasks_in_class.description: 52 stamps total, 37 with famous persons — find how many show monuments (52 – 37); find other ways on the number line.
They have 52 stamps and want 75 — figure out how many more stamps they need using the number line.
The grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10 each time — mark all beads it will jump on and write the numbers.
Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers.

time_bands.activity: Children work through Let us Do, p.33 ("52 stamps total, 37 with famous persons — find how many show monuments (52 – 37); find other ways on the number line....") and Let us Do, p.33 ("They have 52 stamps and want 75 — figure out how many more stamps they need using the number line....") on individual number-line strips. After solving, two or three children share different jump paths so the class sees multiple valid strategies.

Let us Do Q4, p.34 ("The grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10 each time — mark all beads it will jump on and write the numbers....") is worked in pairs. Children mark each landing bead and write the descending sequence. The teacher invites children to notice the pattern in the tens digit across the sequence.

Children complete the jump tables in Let us Do Q5, p.35 ("Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers....") individually. The teacher circulates and asks: 'Can you predict two steps ahead without counting one at a time?'

periods.teacher_notes: The stamp subtraction tasks (52–37 and 75–52) sit on the same number line, so children can see a 'finding the difference' jump as an alternative to a 'take away' jump — highlight this if a child spontaneously uses it. For the backward grasshopper task, children frequently decrement the ones digit rather than the tens digit; having them circle the tens digit before jumping helps. Jump tables with step 9 benefit from a brief discussion of jumping 10 then back 1.

section_titles: Addition and subtraction on the 100-number grid
periods.activity_title: Moving Counters on the Hundred Chart

tasks_in_class.description: Number Grid Game: players roll two dice to form a two-digit number and move a counter forward or backward on the 100 grid; first to reach 91–100 wins.
Use the number grid to find where each player lands: (a) 45+34 (b) 75+56 (c) 30+66 (d) 89+63; show thinking by drawing arrows in the grid.

time_bands.activity: The teacher places a large 100-number grid on the board and demonstrates that moving right adds ones while moving down adds tens. Two children demonstrate a move (e.g. start at 24, move right 3, then down 2) and name the landing number. The class discusses why the grid 'does the same job' as the bead string, which children have used to add and subtract across a range of tasks.

The Number Grid Game from Let us Play, p.35 ("Number Grid Game: players roll two dice to form a two-digit number and move a counter forward or backward on the 100 grid; first to reach 91–100 wins....") runs in pairs. Each pair has a printed 100 grid and a counter. The teacher pauses the game once to ask: 'If you are on 53 and roll a 4 and a 2, is 42 or 24 a better number to move forward? Why?'

Children solve Let us Do Q1(a–d), p.36 ("Use the number grid to find where each player lands: (a) 45+34 (b) 75+56 (c) 30+66 (d) 89+63; show thinking by drawing arrows in the grid....") on their own grid sheets, drawing arrows for each step. A pair who finish early compare arrow paths to see whether they moved tens first or ones first.

periods.teacher_notes: A common confusion at first contact with the 100 grid is moving right for tens and down for ones — children reverse the direction of the larger jump. Establish the rule firmly with a demonstration before the game begins. In the arrow-drawing task, children who reach the end of a row and wrap to the next row often miscount; encourage them to do the tens move first (straight down) and the ones move second (across).
materials: Large printed or drawn 100-number grid (class display)
Individual printed 100-number grid sheets (one per pair)

section_titles: Magic Sums — row and column addition puzzles
periods.activity_title: Nani Maa's Number Puzzle: Rows, Columns, Diagonals

tasks_in_class.description: Observe the completed Magic Sums puzzle; fill three incomplete grids so each row and column adds to the given target; add blue-box and red-box numbers and describe what you find.
Fill the blanks to complete the magic square (3×3 grid with 3, 9, and 6 given).

time_bands.activity: The teacher projects or draws the completed Magic Sums grid from p.37 on the board. Children read out each row total, each column total, and both diagonal totals. The teacher asks: 'What do you notice?' and waits for children to state the equal-sum property in their own words before confirming it.

Children work individually on Magic Sums, p.37 ("Observe the completed Magic Sums puzzle; fill three incomplete grids so each row and column adds to the given target; add blue-box and red-box numbers and describe what you find...."), filling the three incomplete grids. When they finish a grid they check all rows and columns before moving on. After all three are done, they add the blue-box and red-box numbers and write what they find.

Children attempt Magic Sums, p.37 ("Fill the blanks to complete the magic square (3×3 grid with 3, 9, and 6 given)...."). The teacher encourages them to use the given entries as anchors: 'If 3 and 9 are in the same row, what must the third number be?' A brief sharing of solutions closes the unit, with the teacher drawing attention to the diagonal property.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may try numbers randomly at first; prompt them to use the given target sum and work backwards from what is already placed. A frequent error is repeating a digit — remind children that each digit 1–9 appears exactly once across the grid. Children who finish the magic-square quickly can be challenged to swap two numbers and see whether the property holds, building intuition about why the arrangement is 'magic'.
materials: Magic Sums grid sheets or textbook open to p.37

section_titles: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
periods.activity_title: Radishes, Boxes, and Bundles: Going Beyond 100

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate total radishes; draw the 25+36 problem as a box diagram; find the answer using matchstick bundles or the number line; find other ways on the number line.
Estimate the number of carrots in a box of 100 (with 65 tomatoes); circle the bundle of sticks showing the correct count; solve 100–65 on the number line.
Draw a box diagram for 85+67 apples; estimate whether the total is more or less than 100 and explain your reasoning.
Find 85+67 using the number line; find who collected more apples and by how much (85–67).

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the radish context and the box diagram (part-part-whole bar drawn on the board). Children estimate the total radishes before calculating, then work on Let us Do, p.38 ("Estimate total radishes; draw the 25+36 problem as a box diagram; find the answer using matchstick bundles or the number line; find other ways on the number line...."). Matchstick bundles (or bundled straws) are available on each table for children to group and regroup physically.

Children work through p.39 ("Estimate the number of carrots in a box of 100 (with 65 tomatoes); circle the bundle of sticks showing the correct count; solve 100–65 on the number line...."). After estimating, they circle the correct bundle picture and then confirm the answer on the number line. The teacher presses: 'How does your estimate compare to the exact answer? Were you close?'

Children draw the box diagram for 85+67 using p.40 ("Draw a box diagram for 85+67 apples; estimate whether the total is more or less than 100 and explain your reasoning....") and write their estimate with a reason. They then solve both p.41 tasks ("Find 85+67 using the number line; find who collected more apples and by how much (85–67)....") on number-line strips. Partners check each other's jumps.

periods.teacher_notes: Children working beyond 100 for the first time often stop the number line at 100; ensure number-line strips extend to at least 160. In the box diagram, children sometimes add all four sub-parts instead of only the two parts they need — model the diagram clearly with labels. Estimation before calculation is the key habit this section builds; do not let children skip it even when they are confident of the method.
materials: Bundled matchsticks or straws (bundles of 10, singles)

section_titles: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
periods.activity_title: Word Problems, a Race to 100, and Estimation Matches

tasks_in_class.description: Q1–Q5: Solve word problems (books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants) by drawing box diagrams and using matchstick bundles or number line; make and share your own word problem.
Two-player game: alternate adding a number between 1 and 10 to a running total; first player to reach exactly 100 wins.
Q1: Estimate each expression and match it to 'more than 100' or 'less than 100'. Q2: Solve all the expressions using a number line and write the answers.

time_bands.activity: Children solve the word problems from p.42 ("Q1–Q5: Solve word problems (books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants) by drawing box diagrams and using matchstick bundles or number line; make and share your own word problem....") in pairs. Each pair draws a box diagram before computing. After Q5 they compose one original word problem and swap with another pair to solve.

The Race-to-100 game from Let us Play, p.42 ("Two-player game: alternate adding a number between 1 and 10 to a running total; first player to reach exactly 100 wins....") runs in pairs. Children keep a written running total. The teacher pauses once to ask: 'If the total is 91, what single number would you choose and why?' to surface strategic thinking.

Children complete Let us Do Q1–2, p.43 ("Q1: Estimate each expression and match it to 'more than 100' or 'less than 100'. Q2: Solve all the expressions using a number line and write the answers...."). They write their estimates first, then compute on a number line to verify. A whole-class share identifies expressions that were surprising — where the estimate and exact answer were far apart.

periods.teacher_notes: The word-problem context (books sold, cricket runs, vadas) connects computation to everyday life; encourage children to say what each number in their box diagram stands for, not just write numerals. In the Race-to-100 game, children who reach 95+ and overshoot often do not realise they must land exactly on 100 — clarify the rule at the start. For the estimation-and-match task, children who always estimate 'more than 100' regardless of the expression need prompting to look at the tens digits of both addends first.

items.prompt: There are 14 seeds in all. Meera can see 9 seeds on the table. How many seeds are hidden under the cloth? Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the missing addend: subtract the visible count from the total (14 – 9 = 5).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child act it out with 14 counters and a cloth; stretch: give a new total and a different visible count and ask them to write both the addition and subtraction sentence.

exercise.description: Perform the hidden-seed magic trick with friends; write the number of hidden seeds in the table for six total-and-visible pairs.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Draw dots in the two tens frames below to show 8 + 6. Then write the number sentence. Now cross out 6 dots from the same frames and write the subtraction number sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 + 6 = 14 (first frame full with 10, second frame has 4 dots); 14 – 6 = 8 (after crossing out 6 dots).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fill the first tens frame to 10, place the remaining dots in the second frame, then count the total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a printed tens frame for the child to physically draw dots; stretch: ask the child to write a third sentence using the same three numbers (e.g. 6 + 8 = 14).

exercise.description: Draw the number of dots for 7 balushahi + 5 balushahi and 7 balushahi – 5 balushahi; complete the number sentences.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: Ravi picks 48 tomatoes and Priya picks 39 tomatoes. Draw a box diagram to show this problem. Then write: do you think the total is more than 100 or less than 100? Explain how you decided without working it out exactly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Box diagram shows two parts: 48 and 39, with a whole box on top. The total is less than 100 because 48 is close to 50 and 39 is close to 40, and 50 + 40 = 90, which is less than 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each addend to the nearest ten, add the rounded values, and compare with 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child the printed box diagram outline to label; stretch: ask them to find two numbers that would make the total more than 100 and draw that box diagram.

exercise.description: Draw a box diagram for 85+67 apples; estimate whether the total is more or less than 100 and explain your reasoning.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Arjun picks three number cards: 4, 13, and 9. Which statement correctly uses all three cards?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the two smaller numbers add to the largest number (4 + 9 = 13).

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child does not check whether the sum is larger than both addends; they may be guessing at positions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child subtracts the smaller from the larger but does not check whether the result equals the third card.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child does not understand that the result of addition must be larger than both addends.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child three physical cards and ask them to arrange them until the sentence balances; stretch: ask the child to write one more valid sentence using the same three cards.

exercise.description: Card Game: shuffle four sets of number cards 1–10; take turns opening one card; keep any three cards that form an addition or subtraction statement.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A frog starts at 4 and jumps forward 10 beads each time. Write all the numbers the frog lands on until it reaches or passes 64.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 10 repeatedly to the starting number: 4 → 14 → 24 → 34 → 44 → 54 → 64.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line and let the child mark each jump with an arc; stretch: ask the child what number the frog would land on after two more jumps, and whether it will ever land on 70.

exercise.description: A frog is at 7 and jumps 10 beads at a time — mark the beads it will land on and write the numbers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A grasshopper is at 86 and jumps backward 10 each time. Which list shows its landing numbers in order?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 10 repeatedly from 86: the tens digit decreases by 1 each jump while the ones digit stays at 6.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child subtracts 11 each time (both digits decrease), confusing a jump of 10 with a diagonal move.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child subtracts 1 from the starting number first, then subtracts 10 — treating the first jump differently.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is jumping forward instead of backward, or has misread the starting position.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a number line so the child can draw arcs backward from 86; stretch: ask at which jump the grasshopper first lands on a number less than 20.

exercise.description: The grasshopper at 76 jumps backward by 10 each time — mark all beads it will jump on and write the numbers.

items.section_title: Magic Sums — row and column addition puzzles
items.prompt: A 3×3 number grid uses the digits 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, and two more digits. Each row must add to 12. The first row has 1, 5, and 6. What must the missing numbers in the second row be if the second row is 4, __, __ and must also add to 12? Write the two missing numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two missing digits must sum to 8 (because 4 + ? + ? = 12, so ? + ? = 8). A valid pair from unused digits is 3 and 5 — but 5 is used. Acceptable answer: the two numbers must add to 8; one valid pair using digits not already placed is 2 and 6 — but 6 is used. The unused digits available are 2, 3, 7, 8, 9; a pair summing to 8 from these is 3 and 5 (5 used), 1 and 7 (1 used), or 2 and 6 (6 used) — the cleanest valid pair is 1 and 7, but 1 is used. Correct unrestricted answer: the two blanks must add to 8. If no repetition constraint is stated in the prompt, accept any pair summing to 8 (e.g. 3 and 5, or 2 and 6). Expected answer for teacher: the two missing numbers add to 8; an example is 3 and 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the known number in the row from the target sum: 12 – 4 = 8, so the two blanks together equal 8.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write '4 + __ + __ = 12' and ask the child to find any two numbers that fill the blanks; stretch: ask the child to find all pairs of single-digit numbers that sum to 8.

exercise.description: Observe the completed Magic Sums puzzle; fill three incomplete grids so each row and column adds to the given target; add blue-box and red-box numbers and describe what you find.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A box holds 100 oranges. 58 oranges are red. About how many are not red?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 40 (exactly 42; 58 rounds to 60, so 100 – 60 = 40 as a quick estimate).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 58 to the nearest ten (60) and subtract from 100 to estimate: 100 – 60 = 40.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child reads 58 as the answer without subtracting, or confuses the red count with the non-red count.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child adds instead of subtracts, or anchors to the wrong quantity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child subtracts a rounded 58 from 60 rather than from 100, mixing up the whole and the part.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a bar of 100 squares, shade 58, and ask the child to count the unshaded squares; stretch: ask the child to find the exact number of non-red oranges using the number line.

exercise.description: Estimate the number of carrots in a box of 100 (with 65 tomatoes); circle the bundle of sticks showing the correct count; solve 100–65 on the number line.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: Which expression has a sum of more than 100?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the tens digits of each pair: if the sum of tens digits is 10 or more (here 6+4=10), the total exceeds 100.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may not check the tens digits; 72+25=97, which is less than 100.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may be attracted to larger-looking ones digits; 48+36=84, less than 100.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child adds correctly but makes a tens-digit error; 51+43=94, less than 100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to round both numbers to the nearest ten and add the rounded values first; stretch: ask the child to change one digit in option B to make its sum exceed 100.

exercise.description: Q1: Estimate each expression and match it to 'more than 100' or 'less than 100'. Q2: Solve all the expressions using a number line and write the answers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction within 20 using tens frames
items.prompt: Use a tens frame to find: 7 + 8 = ?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15. Fill the first tens frame to 10 (using 7 and 3 of the 8), then place the remaining 5 in the second frame: 10 + 5 = 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Make ten first: 7 + 3 = 10, then add the leftover 5 to get 15.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have stopped at 7 + 7 or made an off-by-one error when filling the tens frame.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child added one extra, possibly miscounting while drawing dots.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have subtracted instead of adding, or counted 7 + 6.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a printed tens frame and physical counters to place; stretch: ask the child to use the same method to find 8 + 8.

exercise.description: Use the tens frame to solve: (a) 6+8 (b) 5+10 (c) 9–6 (d) 18–9.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: A rabbit starts at 3 and hops forward 6 beads at a time. Fill in the jump table: 3, __, __, __, __, __. Write all six numbers.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 3 on a number line and draw arcs of 6 beads to find each landing; stretch: ask the child to continue the sequence for two more jumps and say whether the rabbit will ever land on 40.

exercise.description: Fill in the jump tables by jumping as instructed for Jump 5, Jump 6, and Jump 9 from given starting numbers.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: Priya has 34 stickers. Her friend gives her 28 more. How many stickers does Priya have now? Use the number line to find the answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 34 to the nearest ten (40, a jump of 6), then jump the remaining 22 to reach 62.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 30 to 65 and mark 34; ask the child to jump to 40 first and count the rest; stretch: ask the child to show a second way to reach the answer using a different set of jumps.

exercise.description: Nandini and Chirag have 22 stamps; Nani Maa's brother gives 30 more — find the total using the ginladi.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the ginladi within 100
items.prompt: There are 61 books in a library. 38 books are about animals. How many books are about other topics? Show your jumps on the number line.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump back from 61: subtract 1 to reach 60, then subtract 20 to reach 40, then subtract 2 to reach 38 — total jumped back is 23.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to count forward from 38 to 61 on the number line and record each jump; stretch: ask the child to write the related addition sentence that checks their answer.

exercise.description: 52 stamps total, 37 with famous persons — find how many show monuments (52 – 37); find other ways on the number line.

items.section_title: Addition and subtraction on the 100-number grid
items.prompt: Kiran is on square 23 on the number grid. She moves right 5 squares and then down 4 rows. What number is she on now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 68. Moving right 5 adds 5: 23+5=28. Moving down 4 rows adds 40: 28+40=68.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Moving right adds ones and moving down adds tens: 23+5+40=68.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a printed 100 grid and a counter to move step by step; stretch: ask the child to find a different combination of right and down moves that also ends on 68.

exercise.description: Use the number grid to find where each player lands: (a) 45+34 (b) 75+56 (c) 30+66 (d) 89+63; show thinking by drawing arrows in the grid.

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A farmer collects 76 tomatoes and 58 cucumbers. How many vegetables does the farmer have in all? Use the number line to find the answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 76 to 80 (+4), then jump 50 more to 130, then jump 4 more to 134.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 70 to 140 and ask the child to jump to the nearest ten first; stretch: ask the child to find how many more tomatoes than cucumbers the farmer has (76–58) on the same number line.

exercise.description: Find 85+67 using the number line; find who collected more apples and by how much (85–67).

items.section_title: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers beyond 100
items.prompt: A shop had 115 bananas in the morning. By afternoon 68 bananas were sold. How many bananas are left? Draw a box diagram and use the number line to find the answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Jump from 68 to 70 (+2), then to 100 (+30), then to 115 (+15): total forward jump = 2+30+15 = 47.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 60 to 120 and ask the child to count forward from 68 to 115 in friendly jumps; stretch: ask the child to check the answer by adding 47+68 on the number line.

exercise.description: Q1–Q5: Solve word problems (books sold, cricket runs, vadas, dried plants) by drawing box diagrams and using matchstick bundles or number line; make and share your own word problem.
